tip: Και του χρόνου (ke tu khrónu = and next year too) is the standard follow-up wish at birthdays, name days and holidays.
The accent on μάς shows it means us, not our: μάς έμαθε (mas émathe = he taught us).
Στης γιαγιάς (stis yiayiás = at grandma's) leaves the word for house unsaid; στης plus a person normally means at their place.
Λαϊκή (laikí = street market) is the everyday short form of λαϊκή αγορά (laikí aghorá = people's market).
Πόσο πάει; (póso pái = how much does it go for) is an everyday way to ask a price at the market.
Δώρο (dhóro = gift) after a quantity means thrown in free: δύο λεμόνια δώρο (dhío lemónia dhóro = two free lemons).
Πιο (pio) before an adjective makes the more form: πιο φτηνά (pio ftiná = cheaper).
The used-to past covers repeated habits: ψώνιζε πάντα (psónize pánda = she always used to shop).
Πόσο έχουν; (póso ékhun = how much are they) is the plural version, for asking about several items at once.
Έχει (ékhi = it has) also works like there is: έχει πολύ κόσμο (ékhi polí kósmo = there are lots of people).
Τα ρέστα (ta résta = the change) is plural-only; there is no singular form for money handed back.
Verbs ending in -αίνω (-éno) mean get more X: from ακριβός (akrivós = expensive) comes ακριβαίνουν (akrivénun = they are getting more expensive).
Καμιά φορά (kamiá forá = sometimes) is literally some time.
Greek makes a price rather than gives one: μου έκανε καλή τιμή (mu ékane kalí timí = he gave me a good price).
Σακούλα (sakúla) is the shopping or carrier bag; a handbag is τσάντα (tsánda), so the two do not swap.
Λεπτά (leptá) means both cents and minutes: δέκα λεπτά (dhéka leptá) here is ten cents.
Δική μου (dhikí mu = my own) takes the gender of its noun, here feminine to match σακούλα (sakúla = bag).
Το περίπτερο (to períptero = the kiosk) is the little street stand selling water, snacks, cigarettes and tickets.
The ending -άς (-ás) often names the person who runs a place: περίπτερο (períptero = kiosk) gives περιπτεράς (peripterás = kiosk owner).
Πενηντάρικο (penindáriko = a fifty-euro note): the ending -άρικο usually turns a number into the name of a banknote.
Και... και (ke... ke) = both... and: και εφημερίδες και περιοδικά (ke efimerídhes ke periodhiká = both newspapers and magazines).
Putting the word for the in front of the more form makes the most: η καλύτερη (i kalíteri = the best).
Εφημερεύει (efimerévi = it is on duty) is the word for a pharmacy taking its turn to stay open at night.
The accent on μού shows it means to me, not my: μού έδωσε (mú édhose = he gave me).
Τα φάρμακά μου (ta fármaká mu = my medicines) carries two accents: μου normally adds a second one when the stress sits three syllables back.
Τι νούμερο; (ti número = what size) covers shoes and clothes alike.
Στο βάθος (sto váthos = at the far end) is how shops point you to the back of the store.
Πάει (pái = goes) also means suits: μου πάει (mu pái = it suits me).
Καθόλου (kathólu = at all) pairs with δεν (dhen = not) for not at all.
Οι εκπτώσεις (i ekptósis = the sales) run in January and July in Greece.
